I found this while working on [JuliaSmoothOptimizers](https://jso.dev), where every solver
quietly asks for a sparse Jacobian or Hessian and I had never really asked how it gets one.
One of the authors, Alexis Montoison, works in the same ecosystem, and the post reads like
someone patiently answering that exact question. It starts from the chain rule, and the
figure of a small convolution's Jacobian, almost entirely empty, made the problem obvious
before any equation did.

The idea that stayed with me is that two columns which never share a nonzero row can be
computed together in one pass, and then pulled apart again. Finding which columns can share
turns into a graph-coloring problem, and the Hessian version borrows its tricks from Powell,
Toint, Coleman and Moré in the 1970s and 80s, long before machine learning cared. The
authors are also careful to say when none of this pays off, which I appreciated more than
the speedups.

[An Illustrated Guide to Automatic Sparse Differentiation](https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2025/blog/sparse-autodiff/),
ICLR 2025 Blogposts.
